summary: Proposes a way to encode Class A IP addresses for ARPANET-style networks like MILNET and ARPANET, and enhancements to the AHIP host access protocol, formerly 1822. The changes enlarge the PSN field, allow logical host names, carry type-of-service information, and let the network give hosts congestion feedback.

plainLanguage.summary: The network's door used to have a small address label. This memo gives it a bigger label and a way for the door to say "slow down, it's crowded."

questions: how does the enhanced arpanet host access protocol work
how does logical addressing work in ahip-e
subtitle: Enhanced protocol for ARPANET host addressing with logical names and congestion feedback.

tldr.problem: The original AHIP protocol limited ARPANET hosts to 256 packet switch nodes (PSNs) per network, and required hosts to use physical addresses that changed when they moved. Hosts had no way to know which of their data flows was causing network congestion.
tldr.mechanism: AHIP-E expands the PSN field to 10 bits (supporting up to 1,024 PSNs), introduces logical names that are independent of physical location, adds type-of-service specification, and provides per-connection congestion feedback from the network to hosts.
tldr.outcome: The protocol is designed in three versions, allowing gradual deployment: version 1 adds logical addressing with minimal code changes, and version 2 adds congestion feedback. Hosts can selectively reduce congested flows instead of having all flows blocked.

today: RFC 1005 is an informational RFC from May 1987 proposing enhancements to ARPANET host access. It was never formally standardized as an Internet Standard and has not been superseded.

sections.title: Overview of AHIP-E
sections.content:
AHIP (the ARPANET Host-to-IMP Protocol, also known as protocol 1822) connects host computers to Packet Switch Nodes (PSNs) on the ARPANET. AHIP-E is an enhanced version that solves a critical limitation: the original protocol could only address 256 PSNs per network (because the PSN field was 8 bits). As networks grew, this became a bottleneck.

AHIP-E makes five major changes. It increases the PSN field to 10 bits, supporting 1,024 PSNs. It introduces logical addressing, so hosts can use names instead of physical locations. It adds type-of-service bits so hosts can specify delay, throughput, and reliability requirements. It provides subnet congestion feedback on a per-connection basis, and it enables precedence level feedback. The protocol is designed to be deployed in three versions, so existing hosts can continue to work while new ones take advantage of the enhancements.
sections.plainLanguage: The old ARPANET protocol could only handle 256 network nodes. AHIP-E handles 1,024 nodes, lets hosts use names like "server1" instead of numbers, and lets the network tell each connection if it should slow down.

sections.title: Extended and Logical Addressing
sections.content:
In the original AHIP, a 24-bit AHIP address maps to an IP Class A address field. The IP address field is divided: 8 bits for the host number, 8 bits (the LH field) unused by the network, and 8 bits for the PSN number. AHIP-E changes this mapping by reclaiming the unused bits.

AHIP-E addresses use a two-bit format indicator in bits 16-17 of the IP address. A physical address starts with 0 in bit 16, leaving bits 8-15 for the host number and bits 18-31 as a 10-bit PSN field (plus 5 don't-care bits). A logical name starts with 11 in bits 16-17, using bits 8-15 as the upper 8 bits of a 16-bit name and bits 24-31 as the lower 8 bits.

The host need only copy bits 8-31 of the IP address into bits 41-64 of the AHIP leader; the PSN interprets them as a physical address, logical name, or reserved format (prefixed with 10). One key advantage: existing IP addresses with the LH field set to zero remain unchanged, ensuring address mapping stability.
sections.plainLanguage: Old addresses were just numbers like "host 5 on PSN 17". New addresses can be names like "mail-server" that the PSN looks up automatically. The host just copies the IP address bits; the PSN does the smart work.

sections.title: Name Translation and Host Services
sections.content:
Logical names are 16-bit identifiers that the PSN translates to physical addresses. A central network administrator assigns names to hosts and updates the PSN's translation tables via the Monitoring Center. A host declares which names it is currently using by sending a Name Declaration Message (NDM) to the PSN; the PSN replies with which names are now effective.

Three translation policies determine how the PSN selects among multiple physical addresses for a name. First reachable searches the translation table in order and uses the first reachable address. Closest physical address uses routing tables to find the lowest-cost destination for the requested type-of-service. Load leveling rotates through the list to spread load.

If a logically-addressed destination host goes down while messages are outstanding, the PSN attempts to reroute via another effective translation before telling the source host. The PSN provides a Name Server Request/Reply message for hosts that want to query the translation table directly, and a Port List Request/Reply for hosts to discover which names they are authorized to use.
sections.plainLanguage: A host tells the network its names (like it might say "I am the backup mail server"). When another host sends to "mail server", the network picks an actual address based on which's fastest, or rotates if there are multiple. If the main mail server crashes, it tries the backup automatically.

sections.title: Quality of Service and Feedback
sections.content:
AHIP-E adds three type-of-service bits (copied from the IP header) to the AHIP leader. Bit 9 (Delay): 0 for normal delay, 1 for low delay. Bit 10 (Throughput): 0 for normal, 1 for high throughput. Bit 11 (Reliability): 0 for normal, 1 for high reliability. Hosts use the same combination of type-of-service, destination name, and handling type to map to a single connection; messages differing in any of these three open separate connections.

The PSN sends three new feedback messages on a per-connection basis. STOP (type 13) means blocking is imminent; the host should stop sending on this connection. SLOW (type 14) indicates subnet congestion; the host should maintain a window of 1 message (wait for the reply before sending the next). GO (type 16) signals congestion has subsided; resume a window of 8. This mechanism allows a host to selectively throttle congested flows instead of being globally blocked.

AHIP-E also handles precedence levels. A Precedence Level Cutoff Change message (type 17) tells the host the minimum precedence level the network now accepts. If a host tries to send below the cutoff, it receives a Network Not Accepting Messages at this Precedence Level error (type 9, subtype 7).
sections.plainLanguage: A host tells the network if it needs fast delivery or high reliability. The network tells each message stream if it should stop, slow down, or resume normal speed. The host stops only the slow streams, not everything.

sections.title: Three Versions for Gradual Deployment
sections.content:
AHIP-E defines three versions, allowing hosts to upgrade gradually. A host declares its version in bits 13-16 of a NOP (no-operation) message; the PSN learns the version and adapts.

Version 0 is the current AHIP protocol unchanged. Version 0 hosts cannot receive new AHIP-E messages or send new message types, and the PSN sets type-of-service bits to zero on replies. Version 1 hosts can use logical names and the 10-bit PSN field, and can specify type-of-service, but will not receive congestion or precedence feedback messages. A version 1 host requires only three software changes: (1) set the version number field to 1 in NOP messages; (2) copy IP address bits 8-31 directly into the AHIP leader bits 41-64; (3) copy IP header bits 11-13 (type-of-service) to AHIP leader bits 9-11.

Version 2 is fully compliant with AHIP-E and can send and receive all new message types, including congestion and precedence messages. All hosts are expected to implement at least version 1 before PSN numbers above 255 and logical names are assigned to the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Old hosts keep working unchanged (version 0). Newer hosts (version 1) can use names and learn about congestion. The newest hosts (version 2) get everything. The network adapts to each host's abilities.
